topic: Security: auth, tokens, secure storage & networking safety

questions.question: Why should a mobile app use the OAuth 2 authorization code flow with PKCE?
options: PKCE lets the app embed its client secret safely, because the secret is hashed before being sent
A mobile app cannot keep a client secret, and PKCE ties the code to a one-time verifier so an intercepted code is useless
PKCE encrypts the access token on the device, so a stolen phone cannot read the token from storage
PKCE removes the need for HTTPS on the redirect, because the code challenge already protects the code
questions.explanation: Anything shipped in an app binary can be extracted, so native apps are public clients. PKCE has the app send a hash of a random verifier with the authorization request and the verifier itself when exchanging the code, so a malicious app that grabs the redirect cannot redeem it. It is not encryption of tokens and does not replace TLS.

questions.question: For signing in with a third-party OAuth provider, collecting the password in an embedded WebView is the recommended approach; Custom Tabs and ASWebAuthenticationSession are only a convenience.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The OAuth best practice for native apps (RFC 8252) is an external user agent: Custom Tabs on Android, ASWebAuthenticationSession on iOS. With an embedded WebView the app can read the password and inject scripts, users cannot verify the real domain, and existing browser sessions are not reused. Many providers, including Google, block sign-in from embedded WebViews.

questions.question: Where should a mobile app store a long-lived refresh token?
options: In SharedPreferences / UserDefaults after Base64-encoding it, so it is not stored as readable plain text
Encrypted with a key held in the Android Keystore, and in the iOS Keychain with a 'this device only' accessibility class
In a constant in the app's code, generated at build time for each user and refreshed with every release
In a plain SQLite table in the app's sandbox, since other apps on the device cannot read that directory
questions.explanation: Keystore keys and Keychain items are protected by the OS (often hardware-backed) and are not included in plain backups when configured correctly. Base64 is encoding, not encryption. The sandbox helps against other apps, but not against backups, rooted or jailbroken devices, or forensic extraction.

questions.question: Your auth server uses refresh-token rotation with reuse detection. What happens when a refresh token that was already used is presented again?
options: The server treats it as possible theft and revokes the whole token family, so both the attacker and the user must sign in again
The server ignores the reuse, because rotation only matters for access tokens and not for refresh tokens
The server returns the same new tokens it issued the first time, which makes refresh safe to retry blindly
The server accepts it once more but shortens the access token lifetime, then rejects any later reuse
questions.explanation: With rotation each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a second use of an old token means two parties have it. Revoking the family limits damage from a stolen token. This is why clients must save the new token durably before using it, or a crash mid-refresh can log the user out.

questions.question: Five parallel requests all get 401 because the access token expired. The server rotates refresh tokens. What should the client do?
options: Retry all five requests with the expired token after a short delay, since the 401 may be a temporary error
Single-flight the refresh: one caller refreshes behind a lock while the others wait, then all retry with the new token
Let each request refresh on its own, since refreshing five times in parallel is the fastest way to recover
Log the user out right away, since several 401s at once usually mean the account has been compromised
questions.explanation: With rotation, five parallel refreshes means four of them present a token already used, which can trip reuse detection and kill the session. A mutex (e.g. inside an OkHttp `Authenticator`, or an actor on iOS) plus a check whether the token already changed avoids this. Retrying with the expired token just produces more 401s.

questions.question: Your team is considering certificate pinning. Which statements reflect the real trade-offs? Select all that apply.
options: Pin the public key (SPKI hash) rather than the leaf certificate, so routine certificate renewals do not break the app
Ship at least one backup pin, e.g. for a standby key or a second CA, so you can rotate keys safely
A bad pin or unplanned key change can lock out old app versions that cannot be updated quickly
Pinning stops an attacker on their own rooted device from inspecting the app's traffic
Pinning replaces normal certificate chain validation, so the system trust store is no longer consulted
questions.explanation: Pinning narrows which keys you trust, which protects against mis-issued or user-installed CAs, but it creates an operational risk if keys change. Someone controlling their own device can bypass pins with hooking tools, so it is not anti-reverse-engineering. Pins are checked in addition to normal validation, not instead of it.

questions.question: Android's Network Security Configuration can block cleartext traffic and declare pins in XML, and iOS App Transport Security requires HTTPS by default, with exceptions declared in Info.plist.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Both platforms let you set transport policy declaratively: `network_security_config.xml` (cleartext is blocked by default for apps targeting API 28+) and ATS keys in Info.plist. Declarative config is easier to audit than custom TrustManager or URLSession delegate code. Exceptions should be scoped to specific domains, not applied globally.

questions.question: Your app calls a paid third-party API with a secret key. A security review flags it. What is the right design?
options: Hide the key in native code through the NDK and obfuscate it, so it does not appear in the decompiled dex
Encrypt the key with AES and ship the encryption key in a different class so the two parts are never together
Store the key in BuildConfig or Info.plist and enable R8 / bitcode stripping so it is removed from release builds
Move the call behind your own backend, which holds the key, and authenticate the app to it (optionally with Play Integrity / App Attest)
questions.explanation: Anything the app can use, an attacker with the binary can also use; obfuscation, native code and split keys only slow them down. A backend proxy keeps the secret on the server and lets you rate-limit and revoke per user. Attestation helps reject traffic from modified apps, but it adds to server-side control rather than replacing it.

questions.question: Requirement: the payment token may only be usable after a successful biometric check. Which implementation actually enforces that?
options: Keep the token in EncryptedSharedPreferences and show BiometricPrompt the first time the app is opened each day
Show BiometricPrompt / LAContext, and when the success callback returns true, read the token from regular storage
Hash the user's fingerprint template in the app and use that hash as the key that encrypts the stored token
Encrypt the token with a Keystore key that requires user authentication, used through BiometricPrompt's CryptoObject; on iOS, a Keychain item with biometric access control
questions.explanation: When the key itself is gated on authentication, the OS refuses to decrypt without a real biometric match, so hooking the callback gains nothing. A boolean 'success' check is easy to bypass on a compromised device. Apps never get biometric templates, so the last option is not possible.

questions.question: You are designing session tokens for a banking-grade app. Which choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Verifying the JWT signature in the app and treating that as the authorisation check for sensitive actions
Server-side revocation of refresh tokens on logout, password change or a 'sign out everywhere' action
Short-lived access tokens (minutes) paired with a longer-lived, rotating refresh token
Binding tokens to a device key (e.g. DPoP or a Keystore / Secure Enclave key) so a copied token is hard to replay
A 30-day access token kept on disk, so the app rarely needs to refresh and fails less often on bad networks
questions.explanation: Short access tokens limit the window of a leak, revocable refresh tokens give the server control, and sender-constrained tokens make theft less useful. A long-lived access token cannot be revoked quickly without extra checks on every call. Authorisation decisions must be made on the server; anything checked only on the client can be patched out.
